title: Set up quarterly estimated tax payments
summary: No employer withholding means you owe the IRS directly four times a year. Failure to pay enough each quarter triggers underpayment penalties.
detailsHtml:
The safe harbor rule

To avoid underpayment penalties, you generally must pay (via quarterly estimates plus any withholding) either 100% of your prior year's tax liability (110% if your AGI exceeded $150,000) OR 90% of your current year's tax liability — whichever is smaller. Most contractors target the prior-year safe harbor because it's a known number.

Quarterly deadlines: Q1: April 15 Q2: June 15 Q3: September 15 Q4: January 15 of following year

The combined tax burden

Self-employment tax is 15.3% (12.4% Social Security up to the wage base of $184,500 in 2026, plus 2.9% Medicare with no cap, plus 0.9% additional Medicare on income over $200K single / $250K MFJ — note these thresholds are statutorily NOT indexed for inflation and have been frozen since 2013, so more taxpayers cross them each year). The 0.9% surtax also applies to W-2 wages above the same thresholds; employers withhold the 0.9% from any single employee's wages over $200K regardless of filing status, which often produces over-withholding for single filers in this range and under-withholding for some dual-earner MFJ couples. Federal income tax stacks on top. State income tax stacks on top of that. A 24% federal bracket contractor in a 5% state effectively pays 15.3% + 24% + 5% = 44.3% on the marginal dollar — far higher than the equivalent W-2 employee, because the contractor pays both halves of payroll tax (the W-2 employer normally covers half).

Set aside 25–35% of gross income for taxes in a dedicated business savings account, ideally on receipt of each payment. The exact percentage depends on your bracket and state, but it's almost always higher than new contractors expect.
